articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.summary: Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.summary: Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.

articles.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open-source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns
articles.summary: Hugging Face executive Irene Solaiman warns that growing cyberattacks on open AI platforms could force tighter security restrictions, threatening the accessibility that makes open-source communities valuable to developers worldwide.

articles.summary: Otter AI just added support for 27 languages and revealed an upcoming feature that can follow along if speakers switch between languages.

articles.title: Aligned separator design improves lithium metal battery fast-charging performance and stability
articles.summary: When using electric vehicles or smartphones, users often experience inconvenience from long charging times and gradually shortening battery life. To increase charging speed and extend usage time, next-generation batteries with high energy density are essential. However, fast charging has had limitations because deposits can accumulate inside batteries, degrading performance and even increasing the risk of fire. A Korean research team has developed a new foundational technology to address this problem by creating a "highway" through which lithium ions can move rapidly inside a battery.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.summary: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.summary: Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.

articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.summary: MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.

articles.title: People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising
articles.summary: Researchers analyzing nearly 150,000 Reddit posts uncovered unexpected symptom reports linked by users to unapproved versions of retatrutide, including increased appetite, sleep disturbances, and elevated heart rates. The findings differ from clinical trial results and highlight how AI could help identify potential drug safety signals that warrant further investigation.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.summary: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.

articles.title: Q&A: How can organizations improve fairness in automated AI systems?
articles.summary: Critical decisions are increasingly being made by artificial intelligence (AI) systems in high-stakes industries like health care, criminal justice and finance, ushering in a wave of ethical and legal concerns over how these systems can be implemented fairly. Now, a new study by a Penn State researcher and collaborators proposes a holistic theory of AI fairness while providing an applicable framework that organizations can use to manage this complicated issue.

articles.title: Australia to adopt 'mandatory' AI safeguards
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence companies will have to abide by new "mandatory" safeguards when operating in Australia, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday.

articles.title: Architected fillers: Shape becomes a design variable for composites
articles.summary: In a recent study, researchers in materials science at Tampere University challenged conventional composite filler shapes by introducing a different approach in which each particle's 3D geometry is designed first, then printed to specification. The research enables decisions to be made on the shape of the filler, not only its material. This approach using architected fillers could pave the way for new solutions in soft robotics, biomedical materials with tailored stiffness and printed scaffolds for tissue engineering.

articles.title: To end 'whack-a-mole' war on AI deepfakes, address the 'ecosystem,' researchers urge
articles.summary: In May 2025, the TAKE IT DOWN Act became the first federal law to address deepfakes and other forms of AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images. The law criminalizes the distribution of "revenge porn," including AI-generated material, and requires social media platforms and other websites to promptly remove the material upon request.

articles.title: Even modest sleep loss may leave people more vulnerable to email scams
articles.summary: Nearly a third of adults in the U.S. do not get enough sleep. A recent surge in attention to this issue raises serious concerns about its long-term health implications, and new research suggests that it can lead to hazardous outcomes, especially in the context of "phishing" emails.

articles.title: Data centers need power—lower-income rural residents pay the price
articles.summary: As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs.
